svg.text: Five dimensions along which cultures differ in handling failure (THT Consulting's 30-year survey, from Riding the Waves of Culture); a company that reconciles them gets
a platform for innovation
1. Control: us or environment?
internal control favours prevention (long contracts, less repeated waste); external
control favours response (adaptable but leaves causes untreated); Emirates learns
from Western pilots who avoid failure and Arab pilots who try it in simulators
2. Rules or relationships?
rule-centred (US, Britain: 70 to 80 percent of Swiss, North Americans, Australians
would not bend rules for friends) versus relationship-centred (BRIC: only 25 to 40
percent put rule above person); a Brazilian showed that a one-time bend can
motivate a friend if the next review is tougher with mentoring
3. Individual or team failure?
Russians most individualistic (nearly 70 percent blame the individual); in an
Indonesian plant the whole group apologised for one worker's error; IBM rewards
salespeople for presenting lessons learned to colleagues (group performance up 30
percent)
4. How much do we identify with failure?
blame the idea not the person: 72 percent of Dutch and 66 percent of Americans, but
31 percent of Indians, 29 percent of Germans, 24 percent of Chinese, 12 percent of
Japanese; AMD added meeting time-outs so Germans could critique privately in German
and share ideas on Post-it notes
5. Status by performance or position?
achieving versus ascribing: a dairy operator hesitated to stop production in the
boss's presence until made supervisor; a US bank in Argentina fixed motivation by
changing secretaries' imported titles to Personal Assistant
Warning on averages
the cultural unit is not only the country: a Japanese car firm may resemble GM more
than Sony; variation arises by function, business line, hierarchy and geography, so
research at many levels before generalising
